hints: Compare the formulas of ethanamide, $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$, and ethylamine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, and think what must be removed as water and what must be added.
walkthrough:
See what changes from amide to amine**
Look closely at $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$ changing to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$. The $\text{C=O}$ oxygen has to leave, and it leaves as $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The carbonyl carbon gains two hydrogens to become $\text{CH}_2$.

Balance with [H]**
You need 4 atoms of hydrogen from the reducing agent in total, two to make water with the oxygen and two to add to carbon. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2 + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

hints: Think about how ammonia, with its lone pair on nitrogen, attacks the electron deficient carbon attached to bromine in bromoethane.
Recall the special solvent and heating method needed to favour substitution by ammonia and to keep volatile ammonia and halogenoalkane in the mixture.
walkthrough:
Picture the attack**
Ammonia has a lone pair on nitrogen, so it acts as a nucleophile. It attacks the $\delta+$ carbon bonded to Br in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ and displaces $\text{Br}^-$. That is nucleophilic substitution.

Remember the conditions**
Use excess ammonia dissolved in ethanol, not water, to avoid substitution by water. Heat under pressure or in a sealed tube keeps the volatile reactants together and speeds up the reaction.

Final answer: mechanism: nucleophilic substitution
conditions: excess ammonia with ethanol, heat under pressure OR heat in a sealed tube

hints: Think about what happens when the ethylamine product itself, which still has a lone pair, attacks another molecule of bromoethane.
walkthrough:
Follow the lone pair again**
The ethylamine just formed, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, still has a lone pair on N. It can act as a nucleophile toward another $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ to give diethylamine, $\text{(CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{NH}$, and then triethylamine, $\text{(CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{N}$.
Final answer: $\text{(CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{)}_2\text{NH}$ OR $\text{(CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{)}_3\text{N}$

hints: Start by recalling that basic strength depends on how readily the lone pair on nitrogen can be donated to a proton.
Compare ammonia with ethylamine by thinking how an ethyl group pushes electron density toward nitrogen.
For phenylamine, picture where the nitrogen lone pair can go when it is directly attached to a benzene ring.
Put the three bases in order by asking which lone pair is most available and which is least available.
walkthrough:
Define what makes a base strong**
A base accepts $\text{H}^+$. For amines that means the lone pair on nitrogen must be donated to the proton. The more available that lone pair is, the stronger the base.

Explain phenylamine is weakest**
In $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$ the nitrogen p-orbital overlaps with the $\pi$ system of the ring. The lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is much less available to bond to $\text{H}^+$.

Explain ethylamine is strongest**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$ the ethyl group is electron donating by the positive inductive effect. It pushes electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more available than in $\text{NH}_3$. So order is phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine.

Final answer: least basic phenylamine < ammonia < ethylamine most basic
Basicity is ability to accept a proton or donate lone pair to a proton.
In phenylamine the N lone pair is delocalised into the benzene $\pi$ system, less available.
In ethylamine the ethyl group is electron donating (+I), increasing electron density on N, more available.

hints: Recall the two stage route from benzene to phenylamine must go through nitration first, so think what the nitro intermediate looks like.
Remember the nitrating mixture and temperature needed to put $\text{NO}_2$ onto benzene.
Think which reducing agent converts $\text{NO}_2$ to $\text{NH}_2$ without affecting the ring.
walkthrough:
Draw the intermediate**
Benzene cannot be directly aminated. First nitrate it to nitrobenzene, a benzene ring with an $\text{NO}_2$ group.

Nitration conditions**
Use a nitrating mixture of concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ at about 25 to 60 $^\circ\text{C}$. This generates $\text{NO}_2^+$ which undergoes electrophilic substitution.

Reduction to phenylamine**
Reduce nitrobenzene with Sn and concentrated HCl with heat. This gives the phenylammonium salt, then alkali releases $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$.

Final answer: Intermediate: nitrobenzene, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NO}_2$
Step 1: concentrated $\text{HNO}_3$ + concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, 25-60 $^\circ\text{C}$
Step 2: Sn + concentrated HCl, heat, followed by alkali to liberate free amine

hints: Recall that the $\text{NH}_2$ group strongly activates the ring so bromine water gives a trisubstituted product, think which positions are 2,4,6 relative to $\text{NH}_2$.
walkthrough:
Use the activation**
The $\text{NH}_2$ group donates electron density into the ring, so phenylamine reacts with excess $\text{Br}_2$(aq) at room temperature without a catalyst. Substitution occurs at the 2,4 and 6 positions to give 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine as a white precipitate.
Final answer: W is 2,4,6-tribromophenylamine: benzene ring with $\text{NH}_2$ at position 1 and Br at 2,4,6 positions

hints: Think what reagent converts a primary aromatic amine to a diazonium salt at 0 to 10 $^\circ\text{C}$.
walkthrough:
Spot diazotisation**
Reaction 2 forms benzenediazonium chloride from phenylamine. This needs nitrous acid generated in situ from sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid, kept cold below 10 $^\circ\text{C}$.
Final answer: nitrous acid, $\text{HNO}_2$, made from $\text{NaNO}_2$ + dilute HCl, below 10 $^\circ\text{C}$

hints: Look at product Y in Fig. 4.2, it contains two benzene rings linked by $\text{N=N}$ with an OH on the right hand ring, so work back what X must supply.
walkthrough:
Read Y backwards**
Y is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N=N}\text{C}_6\text{H}_4\text{OH}$ with the OH para to the azo link. Reaction 4 is azo coupling between benzenediazonium chloride and X. X must therefore be phenol, which couples in the para position.
Final answer: X is phenol, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$

hints: Recall whether phenol couples with diazonium salts in acid or in alkali.
walkthrough:
Match conditions to coupling partner**
Coupling of a diazonium salt with phenol needs alkali such as NaOH. This converts phenol to phenoxide, which couples much more readily. Keep the mixture cold to prevent decomposition of the diazonium salt.
Final answer: NaOH / alkaline conditions, kept cold

hints: Think what highly coloured stable azo compounds such as Y are used for in industry.
walkthrough:
Link colour to use**
Azo compounds like Y are brightly coloured and stable. They are widely used as dyes for fabrics, inks and indicators.
Final answer: dyestuffs / dyes

hints: Start by thinking how many lone pairs the ligand uses to bond to the metal.
Then describe the type of bond formed to the central metal atom or ion.
walkthrough:
Count the donor atoms**
Mono means one. A monodentate ligand like $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ donates only one lone pair from nitrogen.

Name the bond**
That lone pair forms a single dative covalent (coordinate) bond to the central metal atom or ion.
Final answer: A species that uses one lone pair of electrons to form one dative covalent bond to a central metal atom or ion

hints: Picture an octahedral Cu with six positions, three occupied by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and three by $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, and think when identical ligands are next to each other versus opposite.
Recall how to show 3D shape with solid wedges, hashed wedges and straight lines for bonds in the plane.
walkthrough:
Build the cis form**
Draw Cu in the centre with octahedral arrangement. In the cis (fac) isomer put the three $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ ligands on one triangular face so every $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ is 90 degrees to another $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$. Use wedges and dashes to show depth.

Build the trans form**
In the trans (mer) isomer arrange the ligands so two $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ ligands are opposite each other at 180 degrees, with the third at 90 degrees. The $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands fill the remaining three sites similarly.

Final answer: Two 3D octahedral structures of $\text{[Cu(H}_2\text{O)}_3\text{(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_3\text{]}^{2+}$: cis isomer with the three identical ligands on one face (all mutually cis), trans isomer with two identical ligands opposite each other

hints: Count the total number of dative bonds to Cu in $\text{[Cu(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_2\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_4\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Add up the bonds**
Each $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ and each $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is monodentate and forms one bond. With 2 + 4 ligands, total dative bonds = 6, so coordination number is 6.
Final answer: coordination number = 6

hints: Write the $K_{\text{stab}}$ expression for equilibrium 1 with concentrations in $\text{mol dm}^{-3}$ and cancel units of numerator and denominator.
walkthrough:
Derive units**
For $\text{Cd}^{2+} + 4\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{[Cd(CH}_3\text{NH}_2\text{)}_4\text{]}^{2+}$, $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[\text{complex}]}{[\text{Cd}^{2+}][\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2]^4}$$ Units are $$\frac{\text{mol dm}^{-3}}{(\text{mol dm}^{-3})(\text{mol dm}^{-3})^4} = \text{mol}^{-4}\text{dm}^{12}$$
Final answer: units = $\text{mol}^{-4}\text{dm}^{12}$

hints: Remember $K_{\text{stab}}$ is products over reactants with each concentration raised to its stoichiometric coefficient.
walkthrough:
Write products over reactants**
Equilibrium 3 is $\text{Cd}^{2+} + 4\text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{CdCl}_4^{2-}$. So $$K_{\text{stab}} = \frac{[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Cd}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$$
Final answer: $K_{\text{stab}} = \dfrac{[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Cd}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$

hints: Rearrange your expression from (f)(ii) to make $[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}]$ the subject and substitute $K_{\text{stab}} = 6.3 \times 10^2$ with the given data.
walkthrough:
Substitute and calculate**
Rearrange to $[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}] = K_{\text{stab}}[\text{Cd}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4$. Then $$[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}] = 6.3 \times 10^2 \times 0.043 \times (0.072)^4 = 7.28 \times 10^{-4} \approx 7.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$$
Final answer: $[\text{CdCl}_4^{2-}] = 7.3 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$

hints: Think what happens when basic $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ is placed in water containing $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$.
walkthrough:
Connect base to hydroxide**
$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ is basic, so it reacts with water to give $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$. The $\text{OH}^-$ ligands then coordinate to $\text{Cd}^{2+}$, giving the hydroxo complex alongside the amine complex.

Final answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ acts as a base, accepting a proton from water or $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ to form $\text{OH}^-$, which then forms $\text{[Cd(OH)}_4\text{(H}_2\text{O)}_2\text{]}^{2-}$

hints: Recall that a larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means the equilibrium lies further to the right and the complex is more stable.
Compare the three given $K_{\text{stab}}$ values and think about the stability of the aqua ion $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ for which no formation constant is given.
walkthrough:
Pick the largest K**
Larger $K_{\text{stab}}$ means a more stable complex. Of the three values, $5.0 \times 10^8$ for $\text{Cd(OH)}_4^{2-}$ is largest, so it is the most stable.

Identify the least stable**
All formation constants are much greater than 1, meaning every ligand replaces water favourably. Therefore the starting aqua ion $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$ is the least stable.

Final answer: most stable: $\text{Cd(OH)}_4^{2-}$, least stable: $\text{[Cd(H}_2\text{O)}_6\text{]}^{2+}$
$\text{Cd(OH)}_4^{2-}$ has the highest $K_{\text{stab}}$ ($5.0 \times 10^8$), all $K_{\text{stab}} > 1$ so aqua ion is least stable
